entry.title: One HyperTTS exporter for any dataset, and clip directories a corpus …
entry.content:
One HyperTTS exporter for any dataset, and clip directories a corpus can name

The two existing exporters read their own corpus's intermediate TSVs, so a third import meant a
third copy — and every import after it another. The baked reader dataset already holds the guid,
the spelling and the gloss, so reading that serves every corpus and cannot disagree with what
the reader displays. Output is byte-compatible with the existing round trip, since
ms_hypertts_import.py matches audio back by the guid in column one.

Word clip directories were hardcoded to the two original corpora, which meant no third corpus
could ever have pronunciation audio. A dataset now names its own, and sayWord tries the corpus
in front of you first and then every other — a guid is a hash of the spelling, so whichever
corpus recorded a word, the clip is the right one. That is also why 660 of the graded readers'
2,666 forms need no recording at all: they are already voiced under the mini stories or the
course.

Left out of the word export deliberately: 159 Latin-only forms, because a Telugu neural voice
reading "Hogwarts" is a mispronounced English word rather than a pronunciation guide, and these
are the protected names the graded readers keep in Latin on purpose; and 29 the pipeline itself
marked reference-only. 1,818 words and 925 sentences remain, resumable because a form with a
clip is skipped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Import the graded readers, and make a word card answer about THIS occ…
entry.content:
Import the graded readers, and make a word card answer about THIS occurrence

Three chapters of the Prisoner of Azkaban graded readers: 36 sections, 930 sentences, 2,666
word forms, 6,650 occurrences, 260 constructions, in 1.7 MB. The library is now grouped —
Mini Stories, Intensive Course, Discussions, and the book as one heading with its three
chapters inside — because thirty-six scenes listed flat among the mini stories is a list you
scroll past rather than read.

THE OCCURRENCE IS A NEW UNIT IN THIS READER
Until now a card belonged to a spelling, with `sn` holding senses. That was enough while a
gloss was a property of a form. It is not enough here: this pipeline stores the contextual
gloss, the grammatical role and the aligned English phrase on the OCCURRENCE — this word, in
this sentence — and a form recurs across three chapters doing a different job each time.
Flattening that would discard most of what was authored and would lead the card with a note
from some other sentence, which is precisely the defect the graded-reader project's own review
of the earlier import identified.

A token tuple therefore gains a fourth element, the occurrence index. Datasets built before
occurrences existed have three elements, and a missing fourth reads as "no occurrence data,
use the form" — the previous behaviour exactly, so nothing else changes.

The card now answers in the order their data model asks for: what this form means here, which
English it matches, what job it is doing, what base word to look up, and how the form is built
— each morphological part with a plain-English category before its technical label, since a
label only explains anything to someone who already knows it.

Two departures from the mapping they proposed. Protected Latin is lexical: a token carrying
formIds is a word whatever its script, so Harry and Hogwarts get real cards via the
romanisation id fallback rather than going inert as the safe projection suggested. And
romanisation is carried, not recomputed, because te2rom cannot know what their pinned profile
decided about a loanword.

Two fields are deliberately dropped. `resolution` is 'tentative' for all 6,650 occurrences, so
it belongs once on the dataset rather than on every card; and `roleInSentence` is 'unresolved'
for 71% of them, which rendered would put the word "unresolved" on three cards in four and read
as a malfunction rather than as candour. Nothing here is approved: every bundle is draft by its
own manifest, senses say so, and 1,632 unreviewed morphology parts are flagged as such.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Count each offline set once, not once per text a word appears in
entry.content:
Count each offline set once, not once per text a word appears in

The clip lists deduplicated within a story but not across a corpus, so a word occurring in
three mini stories was offered three times: the panel advertised 671 files for the 444 distinct
clips the mini stories actually have, and the progress counter ran against that inflated total.
The download was never wrong — a repeat is a cache hit — but the number is the whole reason the
panel exists, and one you cannot trust is worse than none when you are deciding what to take on
a plane. Now 444, 4208 and 1022, which is what is there.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Work offline: cache the app and its texts, download audio on request
entry.content:
Work offline: cache the app and its texts, download audio on request

The site needed a signal for everything, which makes it useless on a plane. Now a service
worker stores the shell and all three baked datasets on first visit — 2.2 MB, so it happens
without asking — and Stats gains an Offline panel for choosing which audio to keep.

The worker lives at the repo root rather than in reader/, because a worker only intercepts
requests inside its own scope and the reader loads ../STUDY/te2rom.js, ../GRAMMAR_LAB/verbs.js
and ../ministories/lr/*.mp3 — all above itself. Registered from reader/ at scope '../', a
worker inside reader/ would have caught the page and none of its data.

Two caches, and only the shell one carries a version. Audio never changes once generated and
runs to 197 MB, so it lives in an unversioned cache that survives code updates; versioning them
together would re-download a flight's worth of audio because a stylesheet moved.

Range requests are the whole difficulty. Safari does not fetch an audio file, it asks for byte
ranges, and the Cache API cannot store a 206 — pass those through and audio never caches at
all. So the full response is held and sliced here into the 206 the player expects. The
arithmetic is tested against the seven range forms Safari sends, including the clamp when the
requested end runs past EOF and the 416 when the start does.

The download panel reports what it could not get. The first version swallowed every error and
counted the item done, so it claimed "✓ 14 stored" for 15 tracks while story 3 — which fetched
perfectly when asked again — would have been silently absent in the air. A 404 now means the
clip does not exist, which is ordinary for most words; anything else is retried three times and
then named. Clip sets are split per corpus so the course's 147 MB can be declined on its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Give the discussion a full vocabulary, from the generated annotations
entry.content:
Give the discussion a full vocabulary, from the generated annotations

Definitions went from 305 of 1,022 word forms to all 1,022, and English from none of the 141
lines to all of them. The annotation carries a meaning, a morphological breakdown and a note
per word, which map onto slots the reader already renders: senses with their own draft notice,
and a split shown as bold part plus label.

It also fixes a crash that was already pushed. `l.p` is a LIST of [part, label] pairs — the
reader maps over it — and build was assigning the part-of-speech STRING. 116 entries were in a
shape that threw TypeError the moment their word card opened, invisible until a card was
actually clicked, which nothing in the build or the data check does. The annotation's parts are
the right shape for that slot, so the fix and the feature are one change. The caption under it
no longer claims the split was automatic, which was true for the mini stories and not here.

What the importer refuses matters as much as what it takes. This annotator proposes repairs —
నిజే read as నిజమే — and 45 of the 141 translations rest on such a proposed reading rather than
on the words actually in the transcript. Writing those back would replace what was said with
what a model guessed was meant. They are recorded in the notes column instead, to inform a
correction made deliberately, and the transcript is untouched. An annotation whose lines do not
match the segments is refused outright, since its line numbers would point at the wrong words.

Every sense is status=draft, so the reader says it has not been checked by a native speaker.
The annotation says the same of itself: contextual analysis, no dictionary check, no audio, no
native review.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Align lines to the audio by recognising it, not by counting characters
entry.content:
Align lines to the audio by recognising it, not by counting characters

The old timings were off by a median 4.33 s, and 51 of 141 lines sat a full line or more from
where they are spoken. They measured well because the check was the aligner's own assumption
restated: lines were spread by character weight, then scored on how closely duration tracked
character count. A number like that can only confirm itself, and it cannot see being two turns
out. Nothing consulted the audio.

So recognise the audio. What faster-whisper hears is wrong in detail — సాధారనంగా for
సాధారణంగా — but wrong at a known second, which is all an anchor needs to be. Matching is at
character level because a Telugu word carries its case endings inside it: వాళ్ళకి and వాళ్ళు
never match as tokens while sharing a stem that matches exactly. Each matched character is a
position-to-time pair, and a line's boundary is read off the curve through them.

Three things this needed, each found by measurement rather than reasoning:

  - A rate ceiling, which turned out to do most of the work. Recognition skips stretches, and
    the next block it matches can sit 0.11 s after the last while the transcript between holds
    349 characters; interpolating across that pair crushes those lines to nothing. Eight such
    pairs here. Ordering filters cannot see it — the constraint is speed, so anchor pairs are
    rejected above the recording's own average times 1.2. Derived per resource, because a
    constant tuned on one recording is wrong on the next.
  - Pooled recognitions. Two runs mishear different words, so each anchors where the other
    failed: 84 anchored lines to 105.
  - Boundaries as shared state. A minimum span widened onto one row's end runs past the next
    row's start, because both read the same number — the third time that bug appeared.

Verified the only way that has ever worked here: cut spans out of the audio, recognise them
blind, compare with what the line claims to say. Over a fixed 22-line sample, mean character
similarity 82.4% and nothing under 40%, against 69.6% and five weak lines before the ceiling
was derived. Two hypotheses died on that harness — pause-boundary dynamic programming, which
optimised the same circular objective, and disabling the recognizer's voice-activity filter,
which produced fewer words rather than more.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Import the chapter-1 discussion, readable line by line with its audio
entry.content:
Import the chapter-1 discussion, readable line by line with its audio

First real resource through the import path, and it needed three things the tool did not have.

A turn-per-line segmenter. The transcript is 141 utterances with no blank lines and punctuation
on 84 of them, which is what a generated discussion looks like and which neither existing
reader handles: sentences_of() sees one paragraph and merges every unpunctuated turn into its
neighbour. The line break is the only structure the file has, so --lines trusts it.

Alignment from the audio's own pauses. No captions exist, and flat character weight drifts over
sixteen minutes. silencedetect at -40dB finds 146 pauses against 141 lines — the turn
boundaries — so segments are spread over the speech rather than the timeline and each boundary
snaps to a real pause. That bounds the error: a segment can be wrong about where it starts but
cannot drag the next forty with it. A pause can be claimed only once, which is the fix for both
symptoms of one cause — two boundaries choosing the same pause collapsed 8 segments to zero
length, and the minimum span that repaired them ran 8 others past where the next began.

A build step. reader/data/<slug>.js in the shape the reader already consumes. Short because
word identity is already shared: ids.guid('W', form) is the key both corpora use, so 305 of
1,022 forms arrive with a definition, and any word already rated keeps its level, its SRS date
and its clip.

Three collisions surfaced once a third corpus existed, and the middle one predates it:
  - the router's id pattern, [a-z]*\d+, could not express a tag containing a digit, so
    #/story/hp1d1 matched "hp1", found nothing and fell back to the library
  - read state was keyed by story NUMBER, so finishing mini story 1 also ticked course lesson 1.
    Now keyed by id, with bare numeric keys migrated to the mini stories, since that is what
    they meant when written and a collided write cannot be attributed afterwards
  - the library tally read `STORIES.length - ms` as the course count, advertising 65 lessons

Audio re-encoded to mono 64k: 30 MB to 7.9 MB, and speech loses nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Per-chapter keep-in-English briefs for generating audio from one chapter
entry.content:
Per-chapter keep-in-English briefs for generating audio from one chapter

Handing a generator the whole glossary is handing it a haystack: 158 terms, most of which any
given chapter never mentions. The failure mode is not refusal — it quietly preserves the famous
names and transliterates the rest, which is the precise inconsistency the glossary was built to
prevent. So the brief is counted from the chapter's own text and lists only what that chapter
contains: 34 terms for chapter 1, grouped as people, places, institutions, creatures, spells,
Quidditch, invented words.

Classified and detected terms stay in separate sections. The classified ones carry the
glossary's judgement; the detected ones are this script's capitalisation guess and include
false positives. An unclassified name should still stay in English, so the guesses are worth
listing — but not worth presenting as settled. Chapter 1 is the only chapter where that second
list is short; chapter 5 has 67 entries, which is the glossary coverage gap made visible.

bases() moves to module scope unchanged — write_brief needs the same plural folding that
covered() uses, so that Muggles and Muggle resolve to one anchor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: One import path for outside resources, instead of a new pipeline per …
entry.content:
One import path for outside resources, instead of a new pipeline per corpus

The two corpora here each got their own directory and their own tooling — ministories/ with
ms_*.py, intensive/ with ic_*.py. Fourteen tools, of which maybe three hold reasoning that is
really about Mini Stories or about the course; the rest is the same pipeline twice, diverged by
accident. A third copy for the first podcast and the tooling becomes the project. So: one
directory per resource, all the same shape, one tool that walks it — new, segment, align,
analyze, status.

Segmenting from captions rather than from punctuation is the path worth taking, and not for a
subtle reason: sentence-final punctuation does not survive real transcripts. Auto-captions have
none, and a transcript typed from audio keeps it only when the typist bothered. Splitting such
a file on .?! under-splits badly — three minutes of audio behind one timestamp, one rating and
one click-to-look-up. Cues already record where the speech broke, so they are merged up to a
sentence ender or a width budget, which degrades instead of failing. Timings come free and
exact. Without captions, timings are spread by character weight and marked est; a measured
timing overwrites an estimate and clears the flag, because a column asserting the opposite of
what the row holds is the stale-manifest bug again.

analyze answers the question worth asking before spending an evening on an import: how much of
this can you already reach, and how many new words occur often enough (8+) to be learnable from
it at all. A resource where that second number is small is reading practice, not a vocabulary
source.

The reader needed one fix to accept any of this: a dataset now names its own tag and unit noun.
The tag was /Intensive/.test(d.source), a two-corpus test wearing a general one's clothes —
every third dataset comes back 'ms', takes the mini stories' id prefix, and its story 1 becomes
unreachable behind theirs, which is the exact bug that regex was added to fix.

Resource directories are gitignored: someone else's audio, someone else's transcript, the same
call already made for sources/local/ and translate/source/. meta.json carries a rights field so
that question is answered before the effort, not after.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Read the novel's chapter markers instead of guessing from capitals
entry.content:
Read the novel's chapter markers instead of guessing from capitals

The new copy of the source has intact CHAPTER markers, which the old scan had lost entirely —
so split_chapters() was falling back to its all-caps heuristic for every boundary. That guess
is only defensible when the file offers nothing better. An all-caps paragraph mid-chapter is
not rare in this book: Hogwarts' equipment list, the Daily Prophet's headlines. Run on a
marked-up source it found 23 chapters in a 17-chapter novel, cutting at UNIFORM, COURSE BOOKS,
OTHER EQUIPMENT and GRINGOTTS BREAK-IN LATEST.

Markers win when there are two or more of them; the heuristic stays for the old scan. A run
that does not end at 17 now says so rather than writing 23 files and looking successful.

Also writes source/chapters/chNN.txt — the chapter as something to read, hand to a model or
diff against, in the same paragraph-per-line shape read_source() parses, so a chapter file
feeds back through the segmenter unchanged. Gitignored with the rest of source/.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Shuffle every drill lap so the order stops being a cue
entry.content:
Shuffle every drill lap so the order stops being a cue

The panel's list is alphabetical, so lap one was an alphabetical march
and each later lap kept that relative order. The card you just answered
then works as a cue for the next, and a word you only know in third
position is a word you do not know. Fisher-Yates at the start of every
lap, including the lap built from the words you missed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Drill a text's vocabulary as flashcards until every word lands
entry.content:
Drill a text's vocabulary as flashcards until every word lands

Priming a text before reading it wants a different loop from review: no
daily limit, no scheduling, just every word in the list until you have
said you understood it. Words you miss come back after the rest of the
lap, and keep coming back, so a session ends when the text is clear
rather than when a queue runs dry.

Recognise shows Telugu and asks for meaning; Produce shows English and
asks for Telugu, withholding the example sentence and the audio until you
answer, since either would hand you the word. The example is drawn from
the text you are reading and is the shortest line that uses the word — a
forty-word speaker turn teaches a single word badly.

Finding that line needs every lexicon index a guid occupies, not one:
words in both corpora have an entry in each, BY_G is a plain Map and
keeps only the last, and lines index their own dataset — so కథ in a mini
story was illustrated by a lesson about songs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Keep the 150-word reference page, unwired, behind the parked drawer
entry.content:
Keep the 150-word reference page, unwired, behind the parked drawer

Generated by another agent against this reader's own data, and worth
keeping as a lookup: deep usage notes, recognition hints and per-word
sentence breakdowns for 150 high-frequency words, with deep links back
into reader routes that resolve.

Its provenance checks out where it claims a source. All 124 guids it
cites resolve in the reader, and of 132 sourced sentences 126 are
verbatim clauses lifted from longer turns and 6 are whole lines — none
altered.

Two things it should not be trusted on, which is why the drawer entry
says so rather than leaving it to be discovered. 32 of its examples are
newly written Telugu rather than taken from the texts, which is the one
thing this project does not do. And its "lexical sense checked" badge,
on 140 entries, means an agent asserted the sense — not that anyone
verified it; the same status as the batch glosses, with a label that
reads stronger.

Nothing feeds the reader from here. Its word selection would add little
anyway: every target sampled sits in the corpus top 350 and already has
a gloss, which is the band that recurs often enough to stick from
reading. The band that wants deliberate study is 350-1600, which this
does not cover.

150 KB gzipped, one file, no build step.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Commit the course word clips so the speaker button works off this mac…
entry.content:
Commit the course word clips so the speaker button works off this machine

4,251 clips, 74 MB. GitHub Pages can only serve what is committed, so
until now every speaker button in the Intensive Course was dead anywhere
but this laptop — the same reasoning that un-ignored the mini stories'
word clips.

Three lines again, because git will not descend into an excluded
directory: un-exclude the parent, re-exclude the per-turn clips inside
it, re-include only words/. The per-turn clips stay out — the reader
plays intensive/lr/lesson_NN.mp3, which is built from them and is
already committed.

This is a deliberate acceptance of repo growth, not an oversight.
Trajectory is roughly 350 MB once the remaining lessons and stories are
voiced, and re-recording after a translation fix leaves the old copies
in history for good: ministories/lr already carries 26 MB of blobs for a
22 MB working tree after one such round. Day-to-day git is unaffected —
status, commit and push touch the index and new objects, not history —
so the real costs are clone time and permanence. Moving audio to release
assets later is a history rewrite, and the decision to take that on can
wait until the size actually bites.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Sync learning state between devices by code or file
entry.content:
Sync learning state between devices by code or file

Stats gains a Sync panel: copy a code from one device, paste it into the
other. Everything lives in localStorage, which is per-browser, so the
phone and the laptop have each been keeping progress the other has never
seen.

MERGE, NEVER OVERWRITE. Both devices are real. An import that clobbers
works until the first time it runs in the wrong direction and takes a
day's reading with it, so the only operation is a merge — safe in either
direction, twice, or out of order. Verified idempotent: merging the same
code three times leaves byte-identical state.

Conflicts resolve on evidence rather than guesswork. WordLevels already
stores [level, date] per word, so the newer mark wins on its own record.
Only a same-date collision falls back to keeping the further-along mark,
which is the one case the data cannot answer. The cost is a deliberate
downgrade losing to a same-day promotion — a per-word clock would fix it
and is not worth the bytes for something that resolves itself the next
time you touch the word.

Notes are never dropped. Where both sides wrote one and they differ,
both are kept: a card briefly saying two things beats losing a sentence
you wrote. rtt.known is rebuilt from the merged levels rather than
merged separately, so the mirror cannot drift from what it mirrors.

Checking is separate from applying. Import states what it would change
and waits — added, advanced, left alone — because it is the one action
here that can surprise you.

A code is ~49 KB for 4,652 words, a third of the raw JSON, which is
past comfortable pasting; hence Save as file and Load file alongside.
Truncation is the likely failure since chat apps and mail clients mangle
long strings, and it used to surface as the browser's "Failed to fetch".
It now names itself and says to use the file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Fix the doubled vocabulary list, and make clicking a word commit and …
entry.content:
Fix the doubled vocabulary list, and make clicking a word commit and stick

The known-word list was doubled because each dataset builds its own
lexicon, so a word in both corpora has an entry in each — same guid,
same meaning, two rows. One of them carried a story number and the other
did not, which is where "story undefined" came from: only
build_ms_reader recorded a first-met number, and the course builder
recorded neither that nor an occurrence count. The table printed both
straight out as "×undefined · story undefined".

The table now lists one row per word and says where it was met in words:
"story 1 · lesson 13" for a word in both. Merged at render time rather
than at load, because the token arrays index into their own dataset's
lexicon and the arrays cannot be collapsed. 4,652 rows down to 4,493,
none duplicated, none undefined.

Switching to sentence view landed on sentence one however far you had
read, because only playback recorded which line you were on. A click
records it too, so sentence view opens where you were looking.

Clicking an untouched word now commits it at level 2 rather than 1.
Level 1 is blue since the LingQ change, so committing at 1 turned a pale
blue word solid blue — a real change that reads as nothing having
happened. Amber is the point: a word you have touched should look
touched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Restore the progress bar's middle band, which my own change had erased
entry.content:
Restore the progress bar's middle band, which my own change had erased

Not intentional. The bar was known / levels-1-to-4 / untouched, with the
middle band painted var(--l1). Painting level 1 blue to match LingQ
turned --l1 into rgba(127,178,232,.40) against --new-b's
rgba(127,178,232,.38) — the same colour to the eye. The band was still
being drawn; it had simply become invisible against the one beside it,
so a lesson read as nothing but known and new.

Four bands now, because level 1 genuinely is blue and has to stay apart
from untouched: green known, amber for 2 to 4, solid blue for level 1,
pale blue for never seen.

The summary line gains "seen", which is the question the bar exists to
answer — how much of this lesson have I touched at all — and could not
be read off it before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Rating moves one word right; searching stays on Tab
entry.content:
Rating moves one word right; searching stays on Tab

Rating called nextBlue, which looks for the next word still needing a
decision. Re-rating the first word of a sentence whose words were all
already rated therefore found nothing nearby and jumped several
sentences ahead — from sentence 1 to sentence 5 in the reported case.
Correct by its own rule and useless in practice: you were revising that
sentence, not looking for work.

Rating is a cursor now. One word to the right, and on to the next
sentence at the end of this one, whatever the words are marked. Tab and
B still skip ahead to the next word that needs a decision, which is
where a search belongs. Two gestures, one job each.

The cursor itself was never stale — the reported symptom looked like a
focus that had not updated, but the focused word was correct both before
and after the click. What moved wrongly was the rule deciding where to
go next.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Advance to the next word after rating one in sentence view
entry.content:
Advance to the next word after rating one in sentence view

nextBlue looked for spans inside #readtext. Sentence view renders into
.sview, so it found nothing and returned without moving — rating a word
by keyboard there left the focus exactly where it was, which is the one
place it needed to move.

It now walks the sentence in front of you and then steps to the next
sentence that still has an unrated word, so a lesson can be cleared
without reaching for the mouse. Words already rated are skipped, so a
second pass through a lesson only stops on what is left.

It does not wrap in sentence view. Reaching the end should say so rather
than quietly restarting, which looks identical to nothing happening. The
reading view still wraps, because there it shows the whole lesson at
once and wrapping is how you catch what you skipped.

Tab and B are no longer excluded from sentence view — with one
traversal, they are the same "next word that needs a decision" gesture
in both.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Show the same meaning in the lists that the word card shows
entry.content:
Show the same meaning in the lists that the word card shows

glossOf knew about a baked gloss and a verb form, but not about a
registry card or a stem-and-suffix decomposition — and the word card
rendered both of those in sections of its own. So 230 of the mini
stories' 444 words showed a full definition when clicked and nothing at
all in the sentence list, the lesson list and the vocabulary table.

Worst on exactly the words that most need review: a registry card is
written for the words nothing else could gloss, so the ones showing
blank were the hardest ones.

One order now, matching build_ms_reader.best_gloss so the reader and the
Anki export cannot disagree either: your own saved note, the baked
gloss, the registry card, the decomposition, the verb's dictionary form.

The mini stories' lists go from 230 blank to 0. The 168 still blank
across both corpora are 126 OCR fragments, which are not words and have
nothing to say, and the 42 the glossing batch did not finish.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
